overview: Hungary is a landlocked country in Central Europe. Its capital, Budapest, was formed in 1873 when the towns of Buda and Pest, on opposite banks of the Danube, were joined together. Hungarian is not related to most other European languages; its closest relatives include Finnish and Estonian. Hungary joined NATO in 1999 and the European Union in 2004.

geography.text: Much of Hungary is low, flat land in the Pannonian Basin, with the Great Hungarian Plain in the east. The Danube and the Tisza are its main rivers. In the west lies Lake Balaton, the largest lake in Central Europe. Hills rise in the north, but even the highest point is only just over 1,000 metres.

subsections.title: Climate
subsections.text: Hot summers and cold winters on the Great Hungarian Plain.

subsections.title: Wildlife
subsections.text: The plain is home to great bustards, one of the heaviest flying birds, and grey cattle with long horns.

history.text: The Magyars settled the Carpathian Basin in the late 800s, and Stephen I was crowned the first king of Hungary in 1000. Much of Hungary was ruled by the Ottomans after 1526 and later by the Habsburgs. After the First World War it lost about two-thirds of its territory. A 1956 uprising against Soviet control was crushed, and communism ended in 1989.

events.title: First king
events.text: Stephen I is crowned king of Hungary.

events.title: Battle of Mohács
events.text: An Ottoman victory leads to the division of Hungary.

events.title: Austria-Hungary
events.text: Hungary becomes an equal partner in the Habsburg dual monarchy.

events.title: Treaty of Trianon
events.text: Hungary loses about two-thirds of its territory after the First World War.

events.title: Uprising crushed
events.text: A revolution against Soviet control is put down by Soviet troops.

events.title: Border opened
events.text: Hungary opens its border with Austria, helping bring down the Iron Curtain.

government.text: Hungary is a parliamentary republic. Its single-chamber National Assembly chooses the Prime Minister, who leads the government; the President, elected by parliament, has a mostly ceremonial role. Hungary joined NATO in 1999 and the European Union in 2004, and in recent years EU institutions have raised concerns about the independence of its courts and media.

economy.text: Hungary has a large manufacturing sector, especially cars: Audi, Mercedes-Benz and BMW all build cars there, and battery factories have grown quickly. Food, medicines and tourism, including Budapest's famous thermal baths, are also important. Hungary uses its own currency, the forint.

culture.text: Hungarian belongs to a different language family from almost all its neighbours; its distant relatives are Finnish and Estonian. Hungarian inventors created the Rubik's Cube and the ballpoint pen. Paprika is a key spice, used in dishes such as goulash.

items.title: Rubik's Cube
items.text: Invented by Ernő Rubik in Budapest in 1974.

items.title: Thermal baths
items.text: Budapest sits on more than 100 hot springs.

subsections.title: Food
subsections.text: Goulash, a soup coloured with paprika, is the national dish. Chimney cake, a sweet spiral of dough, is a street favourite.

subsections.title: Music and arts
subsections.text: Composers Liszt and Bartók used Hungarian folk music in their work.

subsections.title: Traditions and festivals
subsections.text: At Busójárás in Mohács, people in scary wooden masks chase winter away, a carnival listed by UNESCO.

sport.text: Hungary has won more Olympic gold medals per person than almost any other country. It is especially strong in water polo, swimming, fencing and canoeing. In the 1950s its football team, the 'Golden Team', was the best in the world.

items.title: Water polo
items.text: Hungary's men have won Olympic gold nine times.
Hungary beat England 6–3 at Wembley, England's first home defeat by a team from outside the British Isles.

didYouKnow: Budapest's metro line 1, opened in 1896, is the oldest underground railway in continental Europe.
Hungarian scientists invented the Rubik's Cube, the ballpoint pen and holography.

keyPeople.name: Franz Liszt
keyPeople.text: One of the first superstar performers of the 1800s.

keyPeople.name: Katalin Karikó
keyPeople.text: Won the 2023 Nobel Prize in Medicine for work behind mRNA vaccines.
